removed.text: When a vampire's grave is opened, its eyes glow red.
removed.reason: ralston1872:p.413 says the opened grave shows a rosy cheek and soft skin; it says nothing about the eyes, and no other cited page gives red or glowing eyes.

downgraded.text: In the Tambof story, the vampire could not enter at gates on which crosses had been branded, but the gates without a cross opened of their own accord.
downgraded.to_text: In the Tambof story, at gates on which crosses had been branded the vampire said "Shut tight!" and drove on, though the gates stood wide open; the barred gates of the last house, which had no cross, opened of their own accord.
downgraded.reason: The page does not say the vampire could not enter: it says the stranger called "Shut tight!" at open gates branded with crosses and went on. 'Could not enter' is an inference; narrowed to what the page reports.

retagged.text: Russian peasants believe vampires exert a baneful influence on the weather, and storms, droughts, famines and cattle-plagues are attributed to them.
retagged.reason: The sentence begins at the foot of p.410 ('In the opinion of the Russian peasant vampires') and continues on p.411; the attribution to Russian peasants is on p.410.

flagged.reason: frombald1725:p.11 names no people; 'Serbs' rests on reading 'Rätzischer Manier' (Rascian manner) of the burial as Serbian. A translation choice, kept.
frombald1725:p.11 prints 'Vampyri' as what 'they' (the villagers) call such persons; the people Serbs rests on the same reading of 'Rätzisch' as /peoples_regions/1.
ralston1872:p.410 labels the form 'South-Russian'; recording that as Ukrainians is an interpretation, consistent with Ralston's 'Little-Russians' but not stated on the page.
The OCR on ralston1872:p.410 reads 'upior or upiry the latfcer being his designation among the Czekhs also'; 'upiry' is most likely 'upir,' with a misread comma, but the printed form is not certain.

afanasyev1869:p.557 prints упырь, citing dictionaries, and speaks of beliefs 'у насъ' (among us) surviving chiefly in the Ukraine and White Russia; attaching the form to Russians rather than to those peoples is a reading of 'у насъ'.

grade_rationale.text: Ralston records the vampire's origins among the Ukrainians and White-Russians on a passage that cites no source.

Ralston's Tambof story, the Serbian and Bulgarian origin beliefs and Karadžić's black-colt test are footnoted to Afanasyev, so on those passages Ralston is not independent of Afanasyev and is counted once with him.
The coffin-lid story in Russian Folk-Tales is taken from Afanasyev's tales and is counted with Afanasyev.
Afanasyev records upyr beliefs chiefly in the Ukraine and White Russia, with a Kharkov Government detail.
Afanasyev's Serbian vukodlak account is given from Karadžić, whose dictionary independently equates vampir and vukodlak.
Machal, citing no one on these pages, records the vampire among the Southern Slavs and gives Polish, Slovenian, Bulgarian and Russian names.
Frombald's 1725 official report records an exhumation at Kisolova of a man the villagers called one of the Vampyri.
The verified entry names ten peoples, so the vampire is attested across multiple peoples by at least five independent authors (Machal, Ralston on his uncited passages, Afanasyev, Karadžić, Frombald).
